title: The Return of the Night Train
text:
Twenty years ago, the night train in Europe seemed to be heading for extinction. Low-cost airlines were offering tickets for less than the price of a taxi to the station, high-speed trains were cutting daytime journey times, and one by one the old sleeper services were withdrawn. Their carriages were often shabby, their timetables inconvenient and their prices surprisingly high. Few people expected them to come back.

Yet in the last decade, night trains have made a remarkable return. New routes now link cities such as Vienna, Berlin, Paris, Amsterdam and Brussels, and several companies have invested in modern sleeping cars with private compartments, showers and electronic keys. On some popular routes, tickets sell out weeks in advance, especially in summer.

The main reason for this revival is concern about the climate. A passenger travelling a long distance by train produces only a small fraction of the emissions of the same journey by plane, and many travellers, particularly younger ones, have become uncomfortable with the environmental cost of frequent flying. Some governments have supported the trend by subsidising new services or discouraging short domestic flights.

But environmental concern is not the whole story. Supporters of night trains point out that they save time in an unusual way: instead of losing half a day at airports, passengers go to sleep in one city and wake up in the centre of another. There is no need to pay for a hotel, and no need to arrive at the station hours before departure. For business travellers, this can mean a full working day at their destination.

The revival still faces serious obstacles. Night trains are expensive to run, because each carriage carries fewer passengers than a daytime train and the staff must work through the night. Different countries use different electrical systems and safety rules, so trains crossing several borders need special equipment and complicated agreements. Delays are common, and a late night train can mean a missed connection or an important meeting.

Whether night trains will become a normal way to travel or remain a pleasant niche depends largely on political decisions about investment and ticket prices. For now, however, many passengers seem happy to rediscover an old idea: that a journey can be part of the experience, not just the time between two places.

questions.prompt: What is the text mainly about?
options: Why low-cost airlines have replaced trains
How to book a cheap night train ticket
Why night trains have become popular again and what problems they face
The history of the first European railways
questions.explanation: The text explains the revival and the obstacles.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 1, which of the following helped to cause the decline of night trains?
questions.explanation: Low-cost airlines offered very cheap tickets.

questions.prompt: The word “shabby” in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to
questions.explanation: Shabby carriages = worn and in poor condition.

questions.prompt: What is the main reason for the revival of night trains?
questions.explanation: “The main reason for this revival is concern about the climate.”

questions.prompt: How, according to paragraph 4, do night trains save time?
options: They do not stop at borders.
questions.explanation: Passengers go to sleep in one city and wake up in another.

questions.prompt: Why are night trains expensive to operate?
options: They use more fuel than planes.
Carriages carry fewer passengers and staff work all night.
questions.explanation: “each carriage carries fewer passengers … the staff must work through the night”.

questions.prompt: The phrase “a pleasant niche” in the last paragraph suggests something that
options: is enjoyed by a small, specialised group of people
questions.explanation: A niche is a small, specialised market.

questions.prompt: Which of these statements would the author most probably agree with?
options: Night trains will certainly replace planes.
Night trains have no real advantages.
Governments should ban all domestic flights.
The future of night trains depends on political choices.
questions.explanation: “depends largely on political decisions about investment and ticket prices”.

questions.prompt: The word “they” in paragraph 4 (“they save time”) refers to
questions.explanation: Night trains save time in an unusual way.
